newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Soft Sweden prices seen sparking lower rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Soft Sweden prices seen sparking lower rates.

text.p: A market survey commissioned by Sweden's central bank showed market participants had lowered inflation expectations in the past three months, which analysts said on Wednesday boded well for more interest rate cuts.
Four analysts said the expectations by pollster Prospera were not a surprise but were lower than forecasts.

Prospera's survey of a group of money market participants, purchasing managers and representatives of employees and employers' organisations, predicted annualised inflation at 1.4 percent in a year, 1.6 percent in two years and 2.0 percent in five years.
All these forecasts were 20 basis points lower than the results of a similar survey carried out in September.
"This looks good. The expectations were about a tenth lower than we had thought," said Swedbank analyst Knut Hallberg.

"This bodes well for a new lowering in the repo rate on December 17 and for a lowering of the interest rate corridor with 50 basis points at the Riksbank (central bank) board meeting on Thursday," Hallberg said.

Prospera's poll, carried out four times a year, is one of the central bank's key analytical tools used in its policy planning and is considered one of the weightiest in Sweden when it comes to forecasting inflation.
Though Hallberg said the forecasts were positive for further rate cuts, he noted that rates were nearing the point at which the Riksbank must be cautious.
"We are getting more and more signs that indicate an upturn in economic trends," Hallberg said. "At some time, the Riksbank should become more cautious."
Another analyst also cautioned that these low inflation expectations could be the bottom.
"The question is how much lower inflation the Riksbank should aim for," he said. "We think inflation has reached the bottom now."
Thomas Niemela, analyst with the Stockholm-based brokerage Aragon, was not surprised by Prospera's forecasts but pointed out that the timing of the polling was important.

"The forecast did not contain any surprises, but we must remember that the answers are influenced by the situation prevailing when the questions are asked and now, inflation is very low," Niemela said.
But he said it was still right to assume that future inflation would be low.
"That is probably the right view," he said. "We have very strong fundamentals in the Swedish economy. Unemployment is the big problem, but that doesn't boost inflation."
A fourth analyst also said the poll was positive but warned of risks if wages turned up in the next couple of years.

"A joyful message ahead of Christmas for the Riksbank," the analyst said. "The risk is now mainly that wage increases will not be in line with inflation if we get an economic upturn in 1997 and 1998."
